425	To test whether the death-avoidance finding generalizes beyond Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, we replicate the counterfactual analysis with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 7 task types ($N{=}70$ episode pairs, 10 episodes per task). The internal strategy dies in 58.6\% of episodes versus 24.3\% for deterministic (death-rate differential $+34.3\%$), compared to $+26.6\%$ for Qwen2.5-7B. Direction consistency is perfect: all 7 task types show higher internal than deterministic death rates (7/7, compared to 10/11 for Qwen). The larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$) and the absence of any internal-preferred episodes (0 vs.\ 9 for Qwen) suggest that Llama-3.1-8B is more vulnerable to hallucination-induced death, amplifying the death-avoidance effect. \paragraph{Seed robustness.}
A full replication with an independent environment seed (seed$=$123, $N{=}220$, 11 tasks, strictly 20 episodes per task; the primary seed$=$42 analysis uses $N{=}245$ with 20--40 episodes per task) yields DAF $= 89.7\%$, within 0.7~pp of the primary analysis ($90.4\%$). Internal and deterministic death rates shift modestly ($45.5\%$ vs.\ $42.9\%$ and $20.9\%$ vs.\ $16.3\%$, respectively), but the asymmetry and its downstream effect on routing signal are stable across seeds. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits zero deaths under both seeds, remaining the sole task with score-based (rather than death-based) routing signal, further confirming that the remaining 10 tasks' signal derives almost entirely from death asymmetry. Death dominance is not a seed artifact.

tool_args.old_string: We test whether agent-level improvement reduces death dominance. Retry gives the agent three attempts per episode without self-correction; Reflexion~\citep{reflexion-2023} adds verbal self-reflection between trials (Table~\ref{tab:agent-improvement}). Retry yields only marginal reduction on death-prone tasks ($43.5\%$ at $N{=}5$ vs.\ $48.0\%$ baseline, $\Delta = -4.5$~pp; see dose-response analysis below). Reflexion reduces death to 31.4\% by rescuing 29.3\% of first-trial deaths (27 of 92), but the gap to deterministic (16.3\%) remains 15.1~pp. Trial~1 death rate under Reflexion (41.8\%) matches the single-trial baseline; the reduction comes from cross-trial self-correction, not from the Reflexion prompt itself. Trial~3 adds minimal rescue beyond Trial~2 (net $+4$). Scaling from 7B to Qwen2.5-72B ($10{\times}$ parameters) moderately reduces aggregate death rate from ${\sim}$51\% to ${\sim}$35\% ($\Delta \approx -17$~pp) across death-prone tasks (Table~\ref{tab:agent-improvement}), but does not approach deterministic-level safety (16.3\%). Task-level variation ranges from $+5$~pp (chemistry-mix, where 72B performs slightly worse) to $-31$~pp (lifespan-longest-lived). This variation suggests that scaling yields large reductions in biological-reasoning tasks ($-15$ to $-31$~pp) but provides no benefit for chemical state tracking (chemistry-mix: $+5$~pp; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}). The 31.4\% in Table~\ref{tab:agent-improvement} covers all 11 tasks; on the 10 death-prone tasks, Reflexion achieves ${\sim}$35\%, the figure reported in the Abstract. Recomputing DAF with 72B as the internal strategy ($N{=}220$) yields $90.9\%$ (95\% CI: $[83.9\%, 97.3\%]$), nearly identical to the 7B value ($90.4\%$); the death-asymmetry label fraction rises from $78.9\%$ (7B) to $84.3\%$ (72B). On death-prone tasks ($N{=}200$), DAF reaches $99.5\%$ ($[98.0\%, 100.2\%]$) with $95.9\%$ of labels driven by death asymmetry. A matched 10-task comparison confirms scale-independence: 8 of 10 death-prone tasks maintain DAF $= 100\%$ at both 7B and 72B; episode-weighted DAF declines only from $100\%$ to $97.5\%$. No task shifts from death-dominated to performance-dominated at $10{\times}$ scale. Scaling lowers death rate but leaves death dominance structurally intact.

tool_args.old_string:
\paragraph{Dose-response analysis.}
To characterize the marginal value of additional trials, we extend both Retry and Reflexion to $N{=}5$ trials on the 10 death-prone tasks ($n{=}200$ per condition; Figure~\ref{fig:dose-response}). Retry is nearly flat: death rate decreases from $48.0\%$ ($N{=}1$) to $43.5\%$ ($N{=}5$), a $4.5$~pp reduction across five trials. Reflexion shows a qualitatively different pattern: a steep initial decline from $47.5\%$ ($N{=}1$) to $34.0\%$ ($N{=}3$, $\Delta = -13.5$~pp, $z = 2.86$, $p < 0.005$), followed by a plateau at $34$--$36.5\%$ for $N \geq 3$ (pairwise $z$-tests $p > 0.5$, Wilson CIs overlapping). That Reflexion at $N{=}3$ ($34.0\%$) converges to nearly the same floor as $10{\times}$ capability scaling ($34.5\%$, 72B) suggests a shared structural bound: both interventions attenuate death but cannot close the ${\sim}$18~pp gap to deterministic execution ($16.3\%$). The contrast illuminates the mechanism: Retry's per-trial conditional death rate remains constant at ${\sim}48\%$, confirming that the agent does not learn between blind retries. Reflexion's per-trial rate declines from $47.5\%$ to ${\sim}31\%$ at Trial~3 before a modest uptick at Trials~4--5; this non-monotonicity is a descriptive observation (Wilson CIs overlap across all $N \geq 3$ conditions) rather than evidence of over-reflexion degradation (per-task breakdown in Appendix~\ref{app:dose-response}).

\paragraph{Dose-response analysis.}
We extend both interventions to $N{=}5$ trials on death-prone tasks ($n{=}200$; Figure~\ref{fig:dose-response}). Retry is nearly flat ($48.0\% \to 43.5\%$, $\Delta = -4.5$~pp over five trials). Reflexion drops steeply to $34.0\%$ at $N{=}3$ ($\Delta = -13.5$~pp, $p < 0.005$) then plateaus ($34$--$36.5\%$ for $N \geq 3$, pairwise $p > 0.5$). Retry's per-trial conditional death rate stays constant at ${\sim}48\%$; Reflexion's declines to ${\sim}31\%$ by Trial~3 (per-task breakdown in Appendix~\ref{app:dose-response}).

tool_args.old_string: We probe whether counterfactual labels can train a step-level router, as a diagnostic of label informativeness. The primary bound on performance is the oracle margin: only 2.89 points separate the oracle ($-6.58$) from always-deterministic ($-9.47$), capping routing upside regardless of router quality. A secondary confound is that ${\sim}27.7\%$ of step-level labels are misaligned with their episode-level assignment, further limiting step-level learnability. These two factors are logically independent: a narrow oracle margin limits routing value even with perfectly accurate labels, while mislabeling degrades learning even if the margin were large. In this setting, the oracle margin is the binding constraint: the 2.89-point ceiling means routing can recover at most modest gains regardless of label quality. An implicit router (Qwen3, LoRA fine-tuned; Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}) is trained at three scales (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B) with identical 4-seed configurations. Step-level balanced accuracy is flat across scales ($56.4 \pm 3.5\%$, $58.2 \pm 4.0\%$, $59.2 \pm 3.5\%$; all within seed variance); step-level discrimination is not capacity-sensitive. At episode level, only 4B exceeds the always-deterministic baseline ($59.0 \pm 1.9\%$, $p < 0.005$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}), while 0.6B ($50.7 \pm 2.6\%$) and 1.7B ($43.1 \pm 1.0\%$) remain at or below chance. The 1.7B dip is robust across seeds (range $41.7$--$44.4\%$). We hypothesize that the 1.7B model has sufficient capacity to memorize death-correlated patterns in the training set but insufficient capacity to learn a generalizable routing policy, resulting in spurious anti-correlation; future work should examine per-class routing decisions to test this hypothesis. This non-monotonic pattern, combined with universally low internal recall, reinforces that learned routing does not scale predictably with capacity at current data scales. Unlike single-step tool-calling, the multi-step nature of this routing problem (10--50 actions with compounding state uncertainty) creates inherent label noise between step-level decisions and episode-level outcomes.

At episode level, only 4B exceeds always-deterministic ($59.0 \pm 1.9\%$, $p < 0.005$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}); 0.6B and 1.7B remain at or below chance. The multi-step nature of routing (10--50 actions with compounding state uncertainty) creates inherent label noise between step-level decisions and episode-level outcomes.

\paragraph{Safe RL.}
\citet{garcia2015comprehensive} survey safe RL methods; \citet{tamar2015cvar} optimize CVaR for risk-sensitive policies; the constrained MDP framework \citep{altman1999cmdp}, Constrained Policy Optimization \citep{achiam2017cpo}, and \citet{crpo-2021} provide formal foundations for enforcing safety constraints. 1	\section{Conclusion}
2	
3	We presented a diagnostic framework for decomposing routing signal in modular LLM agents via episode-level counterfactual analysis. Applied to ScienceWorld (245 episodes, 11 task types), 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry; agent improvement baselines (retry, $10{\times}$ scaling, Reflexion) confirm this is robust. Cross-domain contrasts support framework predictions: MATH shows no routing signal without catastrophic failure; ALFWorld identifies information asymmetry as an alternative mechanism. Replication in permadeath environments (NetHack~\citep{nethack-2020}, Crafter~\citep{crafter-2022}), building on recent LLM agent benchmarks \citep{balrog-2025,netplay-2024}, and evaluation with stronger backbones are the most direct open directions.
4

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
4	A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based science simulation with 30 task types, faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}
5	
6	Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
7	Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
8	More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
9	Concurrent analyses of when and whether to invoke tools~\citep{when2tool-2026,tool-use-tax-2026,to-call-or-not-2026} further presuppose diverse routing signals.
10	The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources (accuracy, latency, capability matching) and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.

tool_args.old_string:
This framework addresses a methodological gap.
The standard approach to generating routing labels, per-step oracle comparison, degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, so no step-level signal exists (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
Our counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.
tool_args.new_string: This framework addresses a methodological gap: per-step oracle comparison degenerates under sparse rewards (97.4\% of ScienceWorld steps produce identical scores regardless of modality; \S\ref{sec:collection}), and keyword-based heuristics fail structurally (\S\ref{sec:baselines}). Our counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes. The framework applies to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes.

tool_args.old_string: A complementary question is whether death-avoidance signal is driven by a few outlier task types or distributed systematically. We quantify this via a Signal Concentration Index (SCI) based on the Gini coefficient over per-task routing signal contributions (formal definition in Appendix~\ref{app:sci}). SCI $\in [0, 1]$: values near 0 indicate uniform distribution (systematic phenomenon); values near 1 indicate concentration in a single type (isolated phenomenon). Results are reported in \S\ref{sec:death-decomp}.
tool_args.new_string: We also measure whether death-avoidance signal is concentrated in a few task types via a Signal Concentration Index (SCI $\in [0, 1]$; Appendix~\ref{app:sci}), reported in \S\ref{sec:death-decomp}.

15:Across 245 episodes, $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$; excluding death episodes, $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$, yielding DAF $= 90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$; at the default $P{=}100$). The penalty-independent death-asymmetry label fraction is 78.9\% (75 of 95 non-tie labels). Given observed $\delta = 0.265$ and $P = 100$, the predicted DAF $= \delta P / (\delta P + \Delta_{\text{nd}}) = 26.5 / 29.37 \approx 90.3\%$, closely matching the observed value; DAF is thus a derived quantity once $\delta$, $P$, and $\Delta_{\text{nd}}$ are known, while the 78.9\% label fraction is the penalty-independent empirical finding. Of these 75, 54 (72.0\%) reduce to ties when the death penalty is removed entirely: in those episodes, both modalities score zero without death, so the only reason one strategy outscored the other was avoiding the $-100$ penalty. Death avoidance is not merely the dominant but often the \emph{sole} discriminating signal between modalities. The remaining 21 death-asymmetry labels involve episodes where the surviving strategy also earned positive score, but the death penalty still accounts for the majority of the score gap.
